working with Classes and Instances

       You can use classes to represent many real-world situations. Once you write
       a class, you’ll spend most of your time working with instances created from
       that class. One of the first tasks you’ll want to do is modify the attributes

args.answer:
**What `__init__()` does**

A function that is part of a class is called a *method*, and `__init__()` is a special method that Python runs automatically whenever a new instance is created from the class [1]. Its name has two leading and two trailing underscores, a convention that keeps Python's default method names from conflicting with yours [1]. In the `Car` class, `__init__()` "takes in these parameters and stores them in the attributes that will be associated with instances made from this class" [4]. So it is the initializer that sets up a new object's state at the moment of creation.

**Why `self` is the first parameter**

`self` is required in the method definition and must come before all other parameters [1]. It must be there because when Python later calls `__init__()` to create an instance, the method call automatically passes the `self` argument — every method call associated with a class passes `self` automatically [1]. `self` "is a reference to the instance itself; it gives the individual instance access to the attributes and methods in the class" [2]. Practically, this means when you call `Dog()` or `Car()` you supply values only for the remaining parameters, since `self` is passed for you [2]. Methods that need no extra information are defined with just the one parameter `self`, and the instances created later get access to those methods [3].

**How make, model, and year are stored**

In the `Car` class the method is defined as `def __init__(self, make, model, year):` with `self` first and the three other parameters `make`, `model`, and `year` [4]. The body assigns them with the `self` prefix:

```python
self.make = make
self.model = model
self.year = year
```

which is the same pattern as `self.name = name`: the value held in the parameter is stored in a variable of the same name that is then attached to the instance being created [2]. Any variable prefixed with `self` is available to every method in the class and can also be reached through any instance made from the class [2]. Variables reachable this way through instances are called *attributes* [3]. Later methods read them back as `self.make`, `self.model`, and `self.year` — for example `get_descriptive_name()` builds one string from the year, make, and model instead of printing each attribute's value individually [4]. When Python calls `__init__()` for a new instance, it stores the make, model, and year values as attributes, and can also set default attributes such as `self.odometer_reading = 0` [5].

**Creating an instance of `Car`**

You call the class as if it were a function, passing a value for each of the parameters after `self`, and Python returns a new instance:

```python
my_new_car = Car('audi', 'a4', 2016)
print(my_new_car.get_descriptive_name())
```

Here the instance is made from the `Car` class and stored in the variable `my_new_car`, then `get_descriptive_name()` is called on it to show what kind of car you have [4]. Because `self` is passed automatically, only `make`, `model`, and `year` are supplied in the call [1][2]. Once a class exists, most of your work is done with the instances created from it, and you can change an instance's attributes directly or through methods that update them [6].
